shell.tail -3 noeol.txt: A file without a final newline: the practice terminal ends the output with one, so the prompt starts on a fresh line (a deliberate display choice).
shell.tail -1 noeol.txt: A file without a final newline: the practice terminal ends the output with one, so the prompt starts on a fresh line (a deliberate display choice).
shell.cat -n noeol.txt: A file without a final newline: the practice terminal ends the output with one, so the prompt starts on a fresh line (a deliberate display choice).
shell.rev noeol.txt: A file without a final newline: the practice terminal ends the output with one, so the prompt starts on a fresh line (a deliberate display choice).
shell.tac noeol.txt: tac on a file without a final newline: GNU glues the last two lines together; ours keeps them apart.
shell.wc < fruit.txt: wc reading standard input: GNU sizes the columns from the file it can see behind the redirection; ours always uses width 7, as GNU does for a pipe.
shell.echo one two | read a b; echo \"[$a]\": Each part of a pipeline runs in the same shell here, so read in a pipeline sets the variable (bash runs it in a subshell).
shell.[[ -f fruit.txt ]] && echo yes: [[ ]] is not supported: the course teaches [ ].
shell.f() { echo hi; }; f: Shell functions are not supported; the parser says so.
shell.case x in x) echo yes;; esac: case is not supported; the parser says so.
shell.find notes -name \"*.txt\": find lists entries in the file system's own order, which differs between machines; ours lists them sorted.
shell.find notes -maxdepth 1: find lists entries in the file system's own order, which differs between machines; ours lists them sorted.
shell.find . -name \"*.txt\" -exec echo {} \\;: find -exec is not supported (use a pipe to xargs).
shell.type ls cd: The practice computer keeps its commands in /bin; the host's are in /usr/bin.
shell.which ls: The practice computer keeps its commands in /bin; the host's are in /usr/bin.
shell.tree notes: tree is not installed on the machine running the test; ours has it.
shell.echo ~/notes ~student: ~student: the practice computer has a user called student; the machine running the test does not.
shell.echo $0: $0 is the script file on the real side (the test runs each case as a script) and bash in the terminal.
shell.echo ${#HOME}: HOME is a temporary directory on the real side, so its length differs.
shell.echo ${s/a/b}; echo after: ${var/pattern/replacement} is not supported: it reports a bad substitution.
shell.): Run as a script, bash also echoes the offending line; at the prompt it prints only the message, as ours does.
